Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-56 Filed 03/02/26 Page 2 of 29 UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT EASTERN DISTRICT OF LOUISIANA KATHLEEN MOLLER, * * Plaintiff, * v. * CIVIL ACTION NO. * 2:24-CV-228-WBV-DPC MARTIAN SALES, INC.; JOPEN, * LLC; JOHNSON FOODS, LLC; LP * THE HONORABLE WENDY B. VITTER IND., LLC; CAG HOLDINGS, LLC; * RMH HOLDINGS, LLC; ABC * MAGISTRATE JUDGE DONNA PHILLIPS INSURANCE COMPANY and John * CURRAULT Does 1-4, * * Defendants. EXPERT REPORT OF ALLEN L. DOLLAR, MD, FACC, FACP 1. I have been asked by counsel for the Defendant to review the medical records of Harmony Moller and to formulate opinions as to her cause of death. My fees for reviewing materials, preparing my report, and testifying at a deposition are $700/hour. My fees for trial testimony are $6,000/day. My compensation is neither contingent on the outcome of this matter nor the conclusions reached in this report. 2. In background for my qualifications to render an opinion: I am a board-certified cardiologist with 33 years in clinical practice. I am employed as an Associate Professor of Medicine, Division of Cardiology, in the Emory University School of Medicine. My current CV is attached as Appendix A, and my list of materials considered is attached as Appendix B. My list of prior cases in which I have testified is attached as Appendix C. CLINICAL SUMMARY 3. Harmony Moller was 36 years old at the time of her death on February 6, 2023. She had no significant past medical history. On the day of Ms. Moller’s death, her mother, 1 ND 80231801 2

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-56 Filed 03/02/26 Page 3 of 29 Kathleen Moller found her daughter unresponsive and called 911. The EMS crew attempted to resuscitate her, but their efforts were to no avail, and she was pronounced dead at the scene. 4. Her autopsy, apart from her heart, had no findings suggestive of a cause of death. 5. Toxicology reports from NMS Labs revealed the presence of caffeine, naloxone, THC, diphenhydramine, and promethazine. Mitragynine was present in a concentration of 150 ng/mL. 6. Toxicology reports from UCSF Clinical Toxicology revealed mitragynine was present in a concentration of 158 ng/mL. 7. The cardiac portion of the autopsy revealed that her heart weighed 421 grams, which is heavier than normal (up to 411 grams would be normal per the autopsy report). The autopsy report also notes “mild biventricular enlargement” meaning that there was enlargement of both ventricles, the bottom chambers of the heart. 8. The autopsy notes: “The left coronary artery arises 5 mm above the left sinotubular ridge with an acute angle of origin. There is an inferior aortic wall flap over the origin of the left coronary artery.” 9. The autopsy report ascribes the cause of death to an “abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff exacerbated by mitragynine.” OPINIONS There is no evidence that mitragynine would exacerbate any propensity of a high takeoff of the left coronary to cause sudden death. 10. The autopsy suggests that mitragynine “exacerbated” the high takeoff of the left coronary ostium, but this association has never been observed, nor has anyone postulated such an association in medical literature. The authors of the autopsy report propose no mechanism 2

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-56 Filed 03/02/26 Page 4 of 29 whereby mitragynine could potentially induce sudden death in someone with an abnormally high left coronary artery. Ms. Moller’s mitragynine levels were quite low. 11. Ms. Moller had mitragynine in her serum at autopsy at a concentration of either 150 ng/mL (according to NMS Labs) or 158 ng/mL (according to UCSF Clinical Toxicology). No serum level of cardiac toxicity has been established for mitragynine, but the levels discovered in her serum were very low. A study published in 2021 (1) assessed regular kratom users for evidence of cardiovascular toxicity through the performance of electrocardiograms and echocardiograms.1 In that study, the subject’s serum levels of mitragynine ranged from a low of 2,500 ng/mL to a high of 22,400 ng/mL. The only cardiac effect discovered was a slight prolongation of the QT interval on the electrocardiogram that only appeared in subjects at the higher ranges of mitragynine levels. Ms. Moller’s level of 150 or 158 ng/mL were less than a tenth of the lowest level found in this study. Young people who die suddenly frequently have no cause found at autopsy. 12. Approximately 10-20% of young adults who die suddenly and unexpectedly will have no explanation for their death found at autopsy. The term for this is Sudden Arrhythmic Death Syndrome. Most, if not all, of these individuals with sudden death and a normal autopsy had electrical disorders of the heart (ion channelopathies) during life. These electrical disorders can often be diagnosed during life with an electrocardiogram (ECG), but young adults often have never had an ECG recorded during their lifetime. It is also the case that individuals with ion channelopathies can have a normal ECG- so called “concealed” channelopathies. 1 Leong Bin Abdullah MFI, Singh D. Assessment of Cardiovascular Functioning Among Regular Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa Korth) Users: A Case Series. Front Pharmacol 2021; 12:723567. 3

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-56 Filed 03/02/26 Page 5 of 29 13. Individuals with ion channelopathies can have fatal heart rhythms triggered by a variety of things including low serum potassium levels and medications that prolong the QT interval on the ECG. Ms. Moller likely had 2 potential triggers for Sudden Arrhythmic Death. 14. As noted in the St. Tammany Parish Sherrif’s Office report, Ms. Moller’s mother reported that her daughter had not been feeling well and was throwing up. Vomiting causes a loss of potassium and often leads to low serum potassium levels. As noted above, low serum potassium can trigger Sudden Arrhythmic Death in susceptible individuals. 15. Ms. Moller had also been taking an anti-nausea medication, promethazine (Phenergan), as this was found in Ms. Moller’s blood at autopsy, and noted in the St. Tammany Fire District EMS records and on statements made by Kathleen Moller, Ms. Moller’s mother, on police bodycam footage. Promethazine is known to prolong the QT interval on the ECG. Also as noted above, a prolonged QT interval can trigger Sudden Arrhythmic Death in susceptible individuals.2 REBUTTAL TO PLAINTIFF’S EXPERT REPORTS Rebuttal to Dr. Ronald Wharton’s Report 16. Dr. Ronald Wharton, Plaintiff’s cardiology expert, states that “[s]udden death occurs from either an anatomic or a toxic/metabolic cause. No anatomic cause (traumatic, cardiac, thromboembolic, or neurologic) was identified.” He further asserts that the decedent had “no 2 Rowe EJ, Shugg T, Ly RC, Philips S, Rosenman MB, Callaghan JT, Radovich M, Overholser BR, Schneider BP, Tisdale JE and Skaar TC (2022) Association of QT interval-prolonging drugs with clinical trial eligibility in patients with advanced cancer. Front Cardiovasc Med 9:894623. Jo SH, Hong HK, Chong SH, Lee HS, Choe H (2009) H1 Antihistamine drug promethazine directly blocks hERG K+ channel. Pharmacological Res 60(5):429-437. 4

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-56 Filed 03/02/26 Page 6 of 29 medical history of any condition that would cause a dangerous metabolic derangement,” and concludes that “more likely than not, Harmony Moller died from a cardiorespiratory adverse event induced by consumption of kratom.” 17. Dr. Wharton’s conclusion is incomplete. His statement that there was “no medical history of any condition that would cause a dangerous metabolic derangement” fails to account for Ms. Moller’s documented vomiting on the day of her death. Vomiting is a well-recognized cause of acute hypokalemia, which can trigger malignant ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death, even in individuals without structural heart disease. 18. Additionally, while Dr. Wharton acknowledges that “VT/VF can be precipitated by exogenous substances,” he focuses solely on mitragynine and omits the significance of the promethazine identified in Ms. Moller’s blood. Promethazine is well-established to prolong the QT interval and is a known precipitant of sudden arrhythmic death in susceptible individuals. His failure to address this co-ingestant materially undermines his causation opinion. 19. Finally, although Dr. Wharton cites the mitragynine concentration of 150 ng/mL found at autopsy, he does not contextualize this value within the medical literature. A concentration of 150 ng/mL is substantially lower than levels reported in cases where individuals died with mitragynine detected post-mortem. Dr. Wharton’s report provides no analysis explaining why a comparatively low concentration should be regarded as lethal in this case. Rebuttal to Dr. Josef Thundiyil’s Report 20. Josef Thundiyil, MD, Plaintiff’s emergency medicine and medical toxicology expert, asserts that “[t]he blood concentration of mitragynine was 150 ng/mL, a level sufficient to cause adverse events.” He provides no scientific or medical data to support this conclusion. As 5

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-56 Filed 03/02/26 Page 7 of 29 noted previously, the mitragynine concentration identified at autopsy is substantially lower than levels reported in the literature in cases where mitragynine has been found post-mortem. 21. Dr. Thundiyil further states, “Promethazine was present at a concentration of 18 ng/mL. Said concentration is not consistent with a fatal or toxic dose.” This ignores the well- recognized fact that promethazine, even at therapeutic levels, can prolong the QT interval and precipitate fatal ventricular arrhythmias in susceptible individuals. His assertion addresses only dose-related toxicity and fails to consider pharmacologic mechanisms of arrhythmogenesis. 22. He also opines that cardiomegaly “may be caused by repetitive use of stimulants, like kratom.” There is no medical literature supporting the claim that kratom causes cardiomegaly. This assertion lacks evidentiary basis and does not meet accepted standards for scientific reliability. 23. Dr. Thundiyil failed to mention that Diphenhydramine, found in Ms. Moller’s serum, may be associated with QT prolongation. Medical literature and the Food and Drug Administration indicate there is a correlation in some patients.3 FDA issued a Drug Safety Commuication in 2020 pertaining to consumption of diphenhydramine and heart problems.4 24. Finally, like Dr. Wharton, Dr. Thundiyil fails to address Ms. Moller’s documented vomiting on the day of her death, and the reasonable possibility that this resulted in acute hypokalemia, a well-known trigger of malignant ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. His omission of this physiologic mechanism further undermines the completeness of his causation analysis 3 Shah A, Yousuf T, Ziffra J, Zaidi A, Raghuvir R. (2015) Diphenhydramine and QT prolongation - A rare cardiac side effect of a drug used in common practice. J Cardiol Cases 12:126-129. 4 https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-warns-about-serious-problems- high-doses-allergy-medicine-diphenhydramine-benadryl. 6

Case 2:24-cv-00228-WBV-DPC Document 267-56 Filed 03/02/26 Page 8 of 29 CONCLUSION 25. It is likely that Ms. Moller had an undiagnosed electrical issue with her heart, an ion channelopathy. The combination of promethazine and likely low serum potassium levels triggered her sudden fatal heart rhythm. 26. It is also possible that Ms. Moller’s abnormally high takeoff of the left coronary artery contributed to her death. If so, mitragynine would not have been contributory to death from this cause. 27. The presence of mitragynine in Ms. Moller’s blood was neither causative nor contributory to her death. Sincerely, Allen L. Dollar, MD, FACC, FACP 7
